title: Timeout skew resilience exploratory notes
content:
Goal: understand how per-tenant timeout skew interacts with continuous batching and leads to persistent tail latency / fairness regressions.

Background / motivation:
- Observed occasional days-long windows where a small set of tenants (high latency callers + long token outputs) produce inflated 95/99 latencies for entire batch pool.
- Hypothesis: asymmetric client timeouts and retry backoff patterns create skewed batch composition (lots of long requests that survive timeout threshold), which reduces effective batch throughput and exacerbates tail latency for short requests.
- Not just batch size / timeout tuning — it's an interaction: timeouts -> partial-filled batches -> probe/flush behavior -> starvation.

High-level hypotheses to test:
1) Timeout-skewed workloads increase quantile latency even under same avg throughput compared to uniform-timeout workloads.
2) Adaptive per-slot timeouts that track recent completion CDF can reduce tail latency without sacrificing throughput.
3) Aggressive early-flush for slots with high-probability short-request majority improves short-request P99 but harms long-request throughput; find Pareto frontier.

Experiment matrix (synth + replay):
- Workloads: (A) uniform short (50–100 tokens), (B) mixed-80/20 long(500–800)/short(20–50), (C) skewed timeouts: same mix but client-side timeouts set low for short requests, high for long requests, with retries.
- Scheduler knobs: static-timeout=10ms/25ms/50ms/100ms; per-slot-adaptive-timeout=[off, cdf-approach, ema-mean]; early-flush-thresholds= [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]; soft-priority-demote=[off, small-first, age-weighted].
- Metrics captured: token/sec, batches/sec, fill-rate distribution, per-tenant p50/p95/p99 latency, long-request completion fraction, retry amplification rate, CPU/GPU utilization, queue-occupancy histograms, KV cache hit correlation.
- Traces: microtrace-level annotated events (enqueue, batch-formed, kernel-launch, flush-trigger, deadline). Use synthetic-trace-generator v2 (GH PR above) and production-replay of 2024-08-21 spike window (SCHED-1287).

Initial runs summary (09/15–09/26):
- Run 1 (baseline static-timeout 50ms, no adaptive): mixed workload B produced p99 short-request latency spike up to 4.2x baseline; fill-rate median 0.68 but 10% of batches <0.2 fill. CPU busy waiting increases.
- Run 2 (adaptive cdf per-slot): p99 for short requests improved by ~28%, fill-rate variance reduced; however, long-request tail deferred causing slight 8% drop in throughput for long requests (more preemptions).
- Run 3 (early-flush threshold 0.25): short-request p99 improved ~45% vs baseline, but retry amplification for long-request clients increased 2.1x (observed retries at app layer).
- Run 4 (soft-priority small-first): helped short-request latency but showed fairness churn across tenants; tenants sending mixed-size streams observed oscillation in perceived throughput (tenant-level p50 fluctuated).

Microtrace observations:
- Key path: enqueue -> slot wait -> flush by timeout -> kernel start. Many batches flushed by a single long request exceeding per-slot timeout, causing short requests to be forced late in next batch.
- When client timeouts are shorter for short requests, retries create arrival bursts that temporally align with long-request windows -> burst amplification.
- KV cache misses correlated with long-request batches (long requests tend to be less cacheable) and amplified GPU kernel time by 12–18% on those critical batches.

Quick actionable ideas (pri-ordered):
1) Implement per-tenant deadline-awareness: track per-tenant recent completion CDF and set soft deadlines per request (not hard flush), combined with lightweight preemption hint.
2) Introduce "short-request fast-path" slots: a fraction of slots only accept requests predicted <T tokens based on metadata/past history; keep strict admission to avoid oscillation.
3) Adaptive early-flush annealing: aggressive early-flush during steady short-request-dominant windows, back off when long-request fraction rises; require hysteresis.
4) Add jitter to retry backoff recommendations in client SDK to reduce alignment during partial failure windows (coordinate with devexp).

Open questions / risks:
- Can a fast-path slot be gamed by tenants intentionally mislabeling requests (metadata trust issue)? Need to combine with empirical size-prediction, not just client hint.
- Preemption hints add scheduling complexity: cost of saving/restoring KV cache / prefill state? Investigate preemption overhead vs benefit.
- Observability: need to add tenant-level batch composition histogram to Console (per-route fill-rate over time) before rolling to prod.

Next steps (owner/action):
- Rohan: instrument tenant-level batch composition + per-batch kv-cache-hit-rate (GH: redwood/observability#517). Due 2024-11-10.
- Marcel: prototype short-request fast-path admission (sim only) + parameter sweep. Due 2024-11-24.
- Sofia: coordinate with devexp on client-side backoff jitter RFC and SDK change. Due 2024-11-17.
- Ava (me): run replay of 2024-08-21 spike under adaptive-cdf + fast-path sim and produce consolidated compare table (p50/p95/p99 short/long + throughput). Target 2024-11-03 draft.

Notes-to-self / fragments:
- Check interaction of early-flush with continuous KV prefill optimization (might prefill unnecessary rows).
- Consider per-model quantile for timeouts rather than per-tenant: models with heavy decoding might deserve different handling.
- Ticket SCHED-1302: instrument retry chains — tie client-id + trace-id across retries to avoid double counting in fairness metrics.

References / links:
- Replay job: gs://redwood-replays/2024-08-21-spike/ (partial)
- PRs: redwood/serving-runtime#3421, redwood/sim-workloads#88
- Slack note: #serving-runtime thread (2024-09-10)

Rough conclusion so far: timeout-skew is a second-order but actionable driver of batch pool tail latency; mitigations that are oblivious (single static knob) either harm throughput or create retry amplification. Adaptive, workload-aware multiplexing (fast-path + annealed early-flush + client jitter) looks promising but needs careful guarding against oscillation and incentive gaming.

Unresolved: Need cost-model to quantify long-request throughput loss vs short-request p99 gain (product/solutions tradeoff). Create short spreadsheet next.
